title: VCRI Data Asset Assessment Methodology v1

grades.meaning: Best-in-class data security posture. Documented, enforced, and attested controls across all dimensions. No critical findings. Suitable for high-trust handling of regulated and sensitive data.

Solid data security posture. Documented controls across most dimensions; minor gaps in 1-2 areas with remediation paths defined. Suitable for production handling of sensitive data with stated caveats.
Acceptable for limited handling. Notable gaps in 2-3 dimensions; remediation roadmap required. Not suitable for regulated or high-sensitivity data without compensating controls.
Significant gaps across multiple dimensions. Data-handling risk material; remediation required before sensitive use.
Material failure of data security posture. Handling of sensitive data not recommended in current state.

subcriteria.title: Data source provenance and lineage
anchors: No record of where data originates; lineage is unknown for stored data.
Provenance noted ad-hoc for some sources; no standard and no lineage tracking.
A provenance standard is defined but inconsistently captured; lineage exists for some pipelines only.
Source provenance documented and consistently captured for all in-scope data; lineage traceable end to end through documented pipelines.
All of #3 plus automated lineage capture enforced in pipelines and periodically audited against the actual data estate, with findings documented.
All of #4 plus cryptographic or institutional provenance attestation on ingest (signed manifests, supply-chain attestations), independently verifiable lineage.

subcriteria.title: Data classification and labeling
anchors: No data classification scheme; sensitivity is not labeled.
Informal classification applied by individuals on some datasets; no defined scheme.
A classification scheme (e.g., public/internal/confidential/restricted) is defined but inconsistently applied.
Classification scheme documented and consistently applied to all in-scope data, with labels carried through storage.
All of #3 plus automated classification/labeling enforced at ingest and periodically audited for accuracy and coverage.
All of #4 plus labels drive downstream controls automatically (access, encryption, retention) and classification accuracy is independently validated.

subcriteria.title: Third-party and shared-data trust controls
anchors: Data received from or shared with third parties is ungoverned; no agreements or trust controls.
Some data-sharing arrangements exist informally; no consistent contractual or technical controls.
Data-sharing agreements and trust requirements are defined but inconsistently enforced across partners.
Documented data-sharing agreements and trust controls (scope, purpose, handling requirements) consistently applied to all third-party data flows.
All of #3 plus technical enforcement of sharing scope and periodic audit of partner compliance with handling requirements.
All of #4 plus independent attestation of partner controls (e.g., flow-down audit, signed attestations) and continuous monitoring of shared-data flows.

subcriteria.title: Authentication to data stores
anchors: Data stores accept shared, default, or unauthenticated access.
Individual credentials used ad-hoc; shared accounts and weak/static credentials still present.
An authentication standard is defined (individual accounts, MFA) but inconsistently applied across stores.
Strong authentication (individual identities, MFA for interactive access) documented and consistently enforced across all in-scope data stores.
All of #3 plus centralized identity (SSO/federation), enforced credential policy, and audited authentication logs.
All of #4 plus phishing-resistant/passwordless authentication and independently attested identity controls, continuously monitored.

subcriteria.title: Authorization and least-privilege on data
anchors: Access is all-or-nothing; broad standing access to data with no least-privilege model.
Some access restrictions applied ad-hoc; no defined authorization model.
A role/attribute-based authorization model is defined but inconsistently applied; standing over-privilege common.
Least-privilege authorization (RBAC/ABAC) documented and consistently enforced; access mapped to need.
All of #3 plus periodic access recertification, automated detection of over-privilege, and audited grants/revocations.
All of #4 plus just-in-time/ephemeral access for sensitive data and independently attested least-privilege enforcement.

subcriteria.title: Non-human and service identity for data access
anchors: Services and applications reach data with shared, hard-coded, or long-lived static secrets.
Service credentials managed ad-hoc; secrets sometimes in code or config.
A service-identity standard (per-service credentials, secret storage) is defined but inconsistently applied.
Per-service identities with managed secrets documented and consistently applied; no hard-coded secrets in scope.
All of #3 plus automated secret rotation, short-lived credentials, and audited service-identity usage.
All of #4 plus workload identity federation (no long-lived secrets) and independently attested non-human identity controls.

subcriteria.title: Data minimization and purpose limitation
anchors: Data is collected and retained without regard to necessity or purpose.
Minimization considered informally on some projects; no standard.
A minimization and purpose-limitation policy is defined but inconsistently applied; collection often exceeds stated purpose.
Minimization and purpose limitation documented and consistently applied; collection mapped to declared purposes for in-scope data.
All of #3 plus technical enforcement (collection/field-level controls) and periodic audit that holdings match declared purposes.
All of #4 plus automated purpose-binding (data tagged to purpose, access denied outside it) with independently validated minimization.

subcriteria.title: PII/PHI discovery and inventory
anchors: No inventory of where PII/PHI resides; sensitive personal data location is unknown.
Partial, manually maintained inventory of some sensitive data stores.
An inventory standard is defined; discovery performed inconsistently and the inventory drifts from reality.
A documented PII/PHI inventory is maintained and consistently updated across in-scope stores.
All of #3 plus automated sensitive-data discovery/scanning on a cadence, reconciled against the inventory with findings tracked.
All of #4 plus continuous discovery across structured and unstructured stores, with inventory completeness independently validated.

subcriteria.title: Consent and data-subject-rights handling (DSAR)
anchors: No mechanism to capture consent or fulfill data-subject requests (access, deletion, correction).
Requests handled ad-hoc and manually with no defined process or tracking.
A DSAR/consent process is defined but inconsistently followed; fulfillment is slow and partly manual.
Documented consent capture and DSAR fulfillment process consistently applied within required timelines.
All of #3 plus tooling that locates subject data across stores, tracks request SLAs, and is audited for timeliness/completeness.
All of #4 plus largely automated, verifiable end-to-end DSAR fulfillment with independent attestation of completeness.

subcriteria.title: Encryption at rest and in transit
anchors: Sensitive data is stored and transmitted in cleartext.
Encryption applied ad-hoc to some stores/links; no standard and gaps common.
An encryption standard (at rest and in transit) is defined but inconsistently applied across the estate.
Strong encryption at rest and in transit (current algorithms, TLS in transit) documented and consistently applied to all in-scope data.
All of #3 plus enforced encryption policy (deny-unencrypted), and periodic audit/scanning that confirms coverage.
All of #4 plus advanced protections where warranted (field-level/tokenization, mutual TLS) and independently attested encryption coverage.

subcriteria.title: Key management
anchors: Keys are hard-coded, shared, or stored alongside the data they protect.
Key handling is ad-hoc; manual, undocumented, with no rotation.
A key-management standard is defined but inconsistently applied; rotation and separation incomplete.
Centralized key management (dedicated KMS/HSM) with documented rotation and separation of duties, consistently applied.
All of #3 plus enforced rotation, access-controlled and audited key usage, and keys separated from protected data.
All of #4 plus HSM-backed/customer-managed keys with verifiable key lifecycle and independent attestation.

subcriteria.title: Data loss prevention and egress controls
anchors: No controls on data leaving the environment; bulk export and exfiltration are unrestricted.
Some egress restrictions applied ad-hoc; no DLP standard.
A DLP/egress policy is defined but inconsistently enforced; coverage has gaps.
DLP and egress controls (allow-listing, content inspection on sensitive data) documented and consistently enforced.
All of #3 plus monitored egress with alerting on anomalous transfers and audited DLP efficacy.
All of #4 plus adaptive DLP tuned on incident data with independently validated egress controls and continuous exfiltration monitoring.

subcriteria.title: Cryptographic standards and crypto-agility
anchors: No cryptographic standards exist; algorithm and key choices are left to individual implementers; no inventory of where cryptography is used.
Some algorithm choices documented informally; no inventory of cryptographic assets (algorithms, certificates, libraries); deprecated algorithms in use with no migration plan.
A cryptography policy (approved algorithms, protocol versions, key lengths) is defined but inconsistently enforced; certificate inventory partial; no agility plan.
Cryptography policy documented and applied; an inventory of cryptographic assets (algorithms, certificates, crypto libraries) is maintained; deprecated-algorithm migrations are tracked to completion.

All of #3 plus a maintained cryptographic bill of materials (CBOM) or equivalent across systems, automated certificate lifecycle management, and a crypto-agility plan (able to replace an algorithm or PKI without redesign).
All of #4 plus post-quantum readiness: a PQC migration roadmap prioritized from the CBOM, and independently attested crypto-agility (e.g., a demonstrated algorithm-rotation exercise).

subcriteria.title: Data integrity controls
anchors: No controls protect data from unauthorized or accidental modification; integrity is unverifiable.
Integrity addressed ad-hoc (occasional checks); no standard.
An integrity-control standard (checksums, validation, change controls) is defined but inconsistently applied.
Integrity controls (validation, checksums/hashing, controlled change paths) documented and consistently applied to in-scope data.
All of #3 plus automated tamper/corruption detection and audited integrity verification.
All of #4 plus cryptographic integrity (signed/immutable records where warranted) with independently verifiable integrity assurance.

subcriteria.title: Backup and recovery (RPO/RTO)
anchors: No backups; data loss is unrecoverable.
Backups taken ad-hoc; untested, no defined RPO/RTO.
A backup standard with target RPO/RTO is defined but inconsistently met; restores rarely tested.
Documented backups meeting defined RPO/RTO, consistently performed, with periodic restore testing.
All of #3 plus automated, monitored backups, regularly tested restores against RPO/RTO, and immutable/offline copies against ransomware.
All of #4 plus geographically resilient, independently verified recovery with attested RPO/RTO performance.

subcriteria.title: Retention and defensible deletion
anchors: Data is kept indefinitely; no retention schedule or deletion process.
Deletion happens ad-hoc; no defined retention schedule.
A retention/deletion schedule is defined but inconsistently enforced; stale data accumulates.
Documented retention schedule with defensible deletion consistently applied across in-scope data.
All of #3 plus automated retention enforcement and deletion, audited for completeness including backups/replicas.
All of #4 plus verifiable, attested deletion (certificates/cryptographic erasure) across all copies.

subcriteria.title: Data-store security monitoring and logging
anchors: Data-store access and activity are not logged or monitored.
Some logging enabled ad-hoc; logs unreviewed and not centralized.
A logging/monitoring standard is defined but inconsistently applied; coverage has gaps.
Data-access and activity logging documented and consistently enabled across in-scope stores, centrally collected.
All of #3 plus monitoring/alerting on anomalous data access (SIEM/analytics) with tamper-resistant logs and audited coverage.
All of #4 plus behavioral analytics for data-access anomalies, validated detection coverage, and independent attestation.

subcriteria.title: Data breach detection and response
anchors: No capability or plan to detect or respond to a data breach.
Response is improvised; no documented plan or defined roles.
A breach-response plan is defined but untested and inconsistently understood; notification obligations unclear.
Documented breach detection and response plan (roles, containment, notification obligations) consistently maintained.
All of #3 plus tested response (tabletop/exercise), data-specific detection use cases, and audited notification readiness.
All of #4 plus regularly exercised response with measured detection/response times and independently validated readiness.

subcriteria.title: Data-store vulnerability and misconfiguration management
anchors: Data stores are not patched or checked for misconfiguration; exposure is unknown.
Patching/hardening happens ad-hoc and reactively; no standard.
A patching and secure-configuration standard is defined but inconsistently applied; drift common.
Documented patching and secure-baseline configuration consistently applied to in-scope data stores.
All of #3 plus automated vulnerability and misconfiguration scanning on a cadence, with tracked remediation SLAs and audit.
All of #4 plus continuous posture management (drift auto-detection/remediation) with independently attested configuration.
